section_1.title: Prerequisite Refresher: The Transformation Paradigm
section_1.content: Define a square matrix as a coordinate system reorientation within the same dimension (e.g., rotation/scaling in 2D). Introduce the concept of a 'Linear Map' where inputs are mapped to outputs.
section_1.example: A 2x2 matrix acting on a 2D arrow, rotating it like a compass needle.

section_2.title: Mapping Up: Embedding into Higher Dimensions
section_2.content: Explain the concept of 'Embedding'. A tall matrix (rows > columns) takes a low-dimensional vector and maps it into a higher-dimensional space, effectively acting as an injection.
section_2.example: A 3x2 matrix taking a flat 2D 'stick figure' and placing it into a 3D room, essentially turning the 2D image into a thin billboard in 3D space.

section_3.title: Mapping Down: The Concept of Projection
section_3.content: Explain the concept of 'Projection'. A wide matrix (columns > rows) takes a high-dimensional vector and maps it into a lower-dimensional space, causing information 'compression' or 'flattening'.
section_3.example: A 2x3 matrix acting as a camera: a 3D cat is mapped onto a 2D photographic sensor, where depth is lost in the projection.

section_4.title: Visualizing the 'Transformation Flow'
section_4.content: Synthesize the two concepts using a visual animation flow. Show the transition from 2D -> 3D (Expansion) and 3D -> 2D (Compression). Emphasize that the matrix is the 'bridge' between these differing realms.
section_4.example: A 3D mechanical robot arm folding its reach into a 2D plane controlled by a matrix transformation.

section_5.title: Conclusion: Why Non-Square Matters
section_5.content: Summarize that non-square matrices are the mathematical engines for changing viewpoints, data compression, and feature extraction in machine learning.
section_5.example: A neural network layer represented as a matrix mapping thousands of pixels (high dim) down to a simple classification score (low dim).
